features.description: Full NGDA noun systems apply the image-checked stem and declared class. Gehīersumnes and ręst have singular abstract production; plural morphology is recognition reference without a new count sense.
features.scope_note: Complete selected nominal systems and their assigned senses. Gehīersumnes and ręst plural cells remain recognition reference.

features.description: Fōt has fēt in selected dative singular and nominative/accusative plural; fōt- in other ending-bearing cells. Fōte is an accepted dative alternative and fōtas an occasional plural, not the selected recall form.
features.scope_note: Only the explicitly selected lexical systems; reference cells and unassigned syntax retain their limits.

features.description: Fēond has selected fēonde dative singular, fīend nominative/accusative plural and fēonda genitive plural. Cook and Wright document other dative/plural realizations; do not substitute the genitive -endra of a different -end family.
features.scope_note: Only the explicitly selected lexical systems; reference cells and unassigned syntax retain their limits.

features.description: Hęre and sciphęre have the complete selected ordinary -e masculine pattern. Cook44.2 explicitly permits expanded hęrg-/hęrig- before singular endings and hęrg-/hęrig-/hęrige- before plural endings; apply the same rule within sciphęre. Variants are accepted without testing independent recall.
features.scope_note: Only the explicitly selected lexical systems; reference cells and unassigned syntax retain their limits.

features.description: Ēðel, sāwol and wǣpen have ending-bearing ēðl-, sāwl- and wǣpn-. Hærfest and pęning retain the medial vowel; the short second syllable is required for the ordinary syncope rule. Wǣpnu is the selected plural beside explicit wǣp(e)n alternatives.
features.scope_note: Only the explicitly selected lexical systems; reference cells and unassigned syntax retain their limits.

features.description: Andwlita and sǣdtīma use the weak masculine pattern. Fǣmne and heorte use the weak feminine pattern, with fǣmn- and heort- before endings. Gehīersumnes doubles final s before endings.
features.scope_note: Only the explicitly selected lexical systems; reference cells and unassigned syntax retain their limits.

features.description: Brād, beald, earg, ēaðmōd and mildheort use the complete long strong model and the weak model. Īsern and ēadig use the selected disyllabic short-model endings, retaining their medial vowel; ēadig has expressly documented optional syncope. Strong/weak choice and ordinary agreement remain prior rules.
features.scope_note: Complete selected strong and weak adjective cells, with their ordinary meanings and agreement. Distinct instrumental positions remain recognition reference.

features.scope_note: Accusative thing promised and optionally dative recipient. No general promise-clause or calling/commanding sense is inferred.

features.description: Complete defined flēon present/preterite indicative system.
features.scope_note: Intransitive flight, or accusative person/thing avoided. This verb is distinct from flēogan, fly.

features.description: Complete defined gemētan present/preterite indicative system.
features.scope_note: Accusative person or thing found. The preterite gemētte is not the past participle gemētt.

features.description: Complete defined geopenian present/preterite indicative system.
features.scope_note: Accusative thing opened, including mouth or eyes; no reflexive/intransitive system is silently established.

features.description: Complete defined grētan present/preterite indicative system.
features.scope_note: Accusative person greeted or taken leave of, extended explicitly to the native-land object required in Cook21.12. Weak grētan is distinct from the strong homonym meaning weep.

features.description: Complete defined cȳðan present/preterite indicative system.
features.scope_note: Accusative thing announced or a ðæt content clause; optionally dative recipient. Selected cȳst follows regular dental loss before -st, cȳð the coalescence of two dentals. Past cȳdde is an attested alternative to selected cȳðde.

features.scope_note: Selected accusative person pursued/persecuted, directly evidenced in Matthew 10.23. Genitive government is also attested and may be accepted if its forms are supported.

features.scope_note: Accusative possession. This is the positive present/preterite indicative only; no imperative, subjunctive, nonfinite or negative system is implied.

Interpret narrative temporal relations from context, clause relations and lexical meaning.
features.scope_note: The two inflected tenses do not map one-to-one to modern English simple/progressive/perfect categories; prior present-for-future remains in force.

features.description: A simple preterite can express action earlier than another past viewpoint.
features.scope_note: Relative anteriority can be made explicit in translation without inventing an Old English compound form.

features.description: Finite habban with a selected transitive past participle expresses a completed action or present/past result.
features.scope_note: The auxiliary agrees with the subject, while the accusative object is the patient of the participle. Selected bare participles are productive. Object-agreeing alternatives are recognized/accepted only within independently supported inflection; no arbitrary causative or intransitive have-perfect is introduced.

features.description: Recognize wesan with an intransitive past participle, specifically gewiten.
features.scope_note: The subject is the departing participant; the phrase is not passive merely because it contains be. Recognize the contextual completed-departure meaning; no unrestricted productive system.

features.description: Recognize wesan with a present participle, specifically sittende.
features.scope_note: Context may motivate simple, progressive or durative English. A simple finite Old English verb may also receive progressive English. No obligatory modern progressive category is inferred.

features.description: Compare an active transitive clause with a supported agentless passive and distinguish event from resulting state.
features.scope_note: Retains prior u07-passive: a passive subject is the affected entity; converting to agentless passive omits any named active agent. Wearð may focus on coming into the condition, wæs on a state or contextually an event. No mechanical became/was rule or fram-agent production.

features.description: Express simultaneous, anterior and intended-later time relative to a reporting viewpoint.
features.scope_note: Prior report subjunctives provide simultaneous sīe/wǣre; anterior hæfde plus selected participle is new. Hæfde is syncretic and context identifies the report function. Wolde plus infinitive retains volition/intention and does not guarantee later realization. Indicative reports may be defensible; no automatic backshift or subjunctive=false.

features.description: Intransitive cease/fail without an expressed genitive object, including seedtime and harvest ceasing or failing in Cook19.16. Earlier genitive cessation remains available for ceasing from rule.
Accusative person killed; distinguishes this lethal sense from previously taught strike/smite.
Seeing is asserted absolutely in the bounded temporal clauses of Cook20.2; no accusative object must be invented.
On+dative with rich/lowly predicates; not physical motion into the noun.
Beforan+dative marks the person before whom someone is sent; extends earlier static location explicitly.
Accusative thing prepared; with the selected past participle, habban retains that accusative patient.
Accusative text or letter written; prior morphology does not itself establish this lexical frame.
Accusative person/thing sent and dative recipient; beforan+dative is a separate ahead-of frame.
Accusative thing thrown, including the assigned hook.
Welig on+dative identifies the thing or resource in which a person, place or productive event is rich; includes harvest rich in fruit.
Ābūtan+accusative, surrounding a person/thing or building around it.
Selected accusative after sending among a group; the directly attested sheep/wolves passage supports this precise use. Dative location is also attested but is not the selected productive frame.
Æt+dative marks the person from whom one learns, as in leornian æt a person.
For+dative identifies the beneficiary in the assigned payment/giving expression; not every for-case or causal use.
Accusative quantity of time expresses duration.
features.scope_note: The supplied forty-years phrase is explicitly local support; this does not establish all numeral systems.

features.description: A numeral plus genitive measure noun can state breadth or height.
features.scope_note: The measure noun fōt is separately taught in full; the twenty-feet quantity remains supplied local support.

features.description: Nǣfre and preverbal ne reinforce one negative meaning.
features.scope_note: Bounded never/never again constructions only; nǣfre mā means never more/again. Do not teach a general negative-pronoun family by implication.

features.description: Predicative genitive identifies a possessor; predicative possessive adjectives agree with what is possessed.
features.scope_note: Distinguish an owner in genitive from ðīn in the gender/number of dæg or niht. Earlier attributive forms are reused with an explicit new syntax milestone.

features.description: Quantitative predicative mā means more in number with a plural subject.
features.scope_note: Selected indeclinable mā plus prior ðonne comparison standard; distinct from earlier adverbial amount of doing. No new māran comparative-adjective system is required.

features.description: On+accusative with adjectival ōðer may have an understood city noun.
features.scope_note: Supplied local on ōðre [ceastre] analysis, using the actual prior ceaster system; no unrestricted nominal ellipsis production is inferred.

features.description: Two separated swā tokens express equality of degree.
features.scope_note: First swā is degree; second swā introduces the standard. Bind each to the actual prior swa-invariant form and its new sense; do not invent a compound form spanning the intervening adjective.

features.description: Swā plus a nominal compares the persons sent to sheep.
features.scope_note: Explicit bounded extension beyond the prior finite comparative clause.

features.description: Recognize the selected past reported condition and possibility in the Picts and Scots passage.
features.scope_note: Source-specific gif ... gefultumoden and ðæt ... meahten are supplied/analyzed in context. This does not promote a complete new conditional or modal subjunctive system.

features.description: Finding accusative rest may include the dative beneficiaries.
features.scope_note: Declared application of Cook160–161 general dative-of-benefit syntax to the bounded Cook21.9 requirement; not a separately quoted dictionary valency witness. It does not require a preposition translating English unto.

features.description: Supplied nāh for the negative possession clause in Cook20.4.
features.scope_note: Reuse already supplied nis for the other local negative clause; full negative systems are not production.

features.description: Ongunnon, began, takes the three infinitives onwinnan, attack, niman, take, and hęrgian, plunder. Pihtas are the Picts, Scottas the Scots; norðan and westan mean from the north and from the west. Hīe refers to the Britons introduced in the separate context; ǣhta means possessions.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Iermdon and hīendon mean afflicted and oppressed. Fela gēara means for many years, with genitive after fela. Hīe can be the Britons as object with the raiders continuing as subject, or the raiders as subject with a Briton object understood; the events do not change. Do not infer a unique case from the spelling.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: On ðǣre unstilnesse, amid that unrest. Onsęndon is the exact prefixed sent; the Britons are now the subject. Ǣrendwrecan, messengers; tō Rome, to Rome. Mid gewritum and wēpendre bēne means with letters and a tearful petition. Wēpendre is a present participle, strong dative feminine singular agreeing with bēne.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: In him fultumes bǣdon, him names the Romans asked and fultumes is the genitive thing requested: help. Hīernes is obedience; singāl is continual; underðēodnes is subjection. Ēaðmōde and singāle are accusative feminine singular. The promise is made by the Britons to the Romans.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Gefultumoden is a preterite subjunctive: if they, the Romans, would help them, the Britons. The following ðæt clause gives the purpose, so that they might overcome their enemies. Meahten is the known preterite subjunctive plural of magan; oferwinnan means overcome. This whole reported condition/purpose sequence is supported locally.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Here the subject of onsęndon is the Romans, while him refers to the Britons. Tō fultume means as help/to their aid. The Old English says they sent an army in the active voice; Cook compares a passive Latin expression. Preserve the actual Old English voice when analyzing it.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Sōna ðæs-ðe means as soon as. On ðis īgland has the accusative goal, to/onto this island. Hīe refers to the Roman force. The following ðā resumes the narrative.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Campedon, fought; wið hiera fēondum, against their enemies, with the source dative after wið. Him micel wæl ongeslōgon means inflicted great slaughter on them. Of hiera gemǣrum means out of their borders, with dative after of; the borders belong to the Britons, Rome’s allies. Āflīemdon means put to flight, reinforcing ādrifon. The enemy object carries on through the coordinated verbs.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Lǣrdon means advised/instructed. Fæsten is a fortification; worhten is the known unprefixed wyrcean preterite subjunctive, here make/build in the advice clause. Him tō gebeorge means for their own protection. The Romans give the advice and the Britons are to build. The source’s wið + dative remains locally supplied.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Sige means victory. Mid micle sige is with great victory: the adjective has the instrumental micle beside the dative noun, as Cook’s note directs. Treat this as a supplied source construction. Hām is the directional home, without a preposition.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Read the three ðā forms in order as when, then, the. The first ðæt is an anticipatory object, this/that, expanded by the later that-clause. Ongēaton means realized; ǣrran gewinnan means former enemies. Gewinnan is a weak masculine plural noun, distinct from the previously supplied neuter gewinn, trouble.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Rōmanisca is the weak masculine adjective Roman. Wæs onweg gewiten means had gone away: gewiten is the past participle of intransitive gewītan. This is an intransitive completed-state/perfect expression, not a passive. The source has plain-e onweg; retain it beside the earlier selected onwęg.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: The returning subject is the Picts and Scots. Sōna means immediately; mid sciphęre, with a fleet. On hiera landgemǣru has accusative plural for movement into their territory; the territory is the Britons’.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Cwealdon means killed. Slōgon and cwealdon reinforce the attack. Ealle is all, naturally people in context; the following neuter ðæt is a headless/collective all that they encountered. A translation all they encountered need not pretend that ðæt is an overt masculine personal relative. Cook’s Latin note reads cædunt.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Swā-swā means just as/like. Rīpe ierðe means ripe crops, a collective feminine accusative phrase. Fortrǣdon, trampled down; fornōmon, destroyed/laid waste. The Britons are treated as a crop that is trampled; the object continues from the preceding clauses.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Foriermdon means ruined/reduced to misery. Hīe is the Britons as object. Mid ealle is the fixed phrase completely/utterly; ealle is instrumental here. The complete phrase is supplied.
features.scope_note: Bounded exact source expression with help visible for every assigned reading task; no independent recall or unrestricted construction milestone.

features.description: Use the fixed phrase æt nīehstan, at length. Its ending is supplied; no general superlative system is required.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Use fēowertig gēara, forty years. This whole duration phrase is supplied; the higher numeral takes the genitive gēara. The duration construction is discussed in this unit.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Rōmane, Romans, is the supplied nominative plural; on Breotone, in Britain, supplies the place-name dative. Retain the preterite target.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Cook prints first (ǣrest). Treat this as a lexical hint: use the previously taught ordinal ǣresta and the needed agreeing form ǣrestan in ðone ǣrestan fisc. The uninflected printed hint is preserved in the prompt.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Twēntig means twenty. Use the supplied measure phrase twēntig fōta; the newly taught genitive of extent also governs seofon fōta.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Use the supplied nominative lēo, lion, after the second swā. No full paradigm of this loanword is assigned.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Bryttas, Britons, is supplied as a nominative plural.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Use nāh, does not own, for the negative possession clause. Cook’s hint sē ðe is retained as printed; the model may use the earlier selected Se ðe, he who. The long-vowel sē is a supplied source spelling, not a newly required paradigm.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Reuse the supplied contraction nis, is not, for the negative be-clause. This local form does not teach the full negative verb system.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Use on ōðre, into another, with feminine accusative singular ōðre and an understood ceastre, city. Cook prints (om. an)other: omit the article an, not the sense another. The city omission is supplied locally.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

features.description: Use the supplied nolde, the contracted negative preterite subjunctive singular of willan, in the reported later intention. Nǣfre mā adds never again; it combines with the negative finite verb. This one supplied contraction does not assign the entire negative paradigm.
features.scope_note: Bounded visible support; no independent recall requirement.

readings.exact_text_without_note_cues:
Ðā ongunnon twā ðēoda, Pihtas norðan, and Scottas westan, hīe onwinnan, and hiera ǣhta niman and hęrgian; and hīe fela gēara iermdon and hīendon. Ðā, on ðǣre unstilnesse, onsęndon hīe ǣrendwrecan tō Rome mid gewritum and wēpendre bēne; him fultumes bǣdon, and him gehēton ēaðmōde hīernesse and singāle underðēodnesse, gif hīe him gefultumoden ðæt hīe meahten hiera fīend oferwinnan. Ðā onsęndon hīe him micelne hęre tō fultume, and, sōna ðæs-ðe hīe on ðis īgland cōmon, ðā campedon hīe wið hiera fēondum, and him micel wæl ongeslōgon, and of hiera gemǣrum ādrifon and āflīemdon; and lǣrdon ðæt hīe fæsten worhten him tō gebeorge wið hiera fēondum; and swā, mid micle sige, hām fōron.

Ðā ðæt ðā ongēaton ðā ǣrran gewinnan, ðæt se Rōmanisca hęre wæs onweg gewiten, ðā cōmon hīe sōna mid sciphęre on hiera landgemǣru, and slōgon ealle and cwealdon ðæt hīe gemētton, and swā-swā rīpe ierðe fortrǣdon and fornōmon, and hīe mid ealle foriermdon.

original_notes.text_original: On the Picts the last edition of Chambers’ Encyclopædia remarks: “Four hypotheses have been formed in regard to the language and origin of the Picts. The first, started by Pinkerton and put by Sir Walter Scott into the mouth of the ‘Antiquary,’ is that they were Teutons, speaking a Gothic dialect; the second, maintained by Dr. Skene, is that they were Gaelic-speaking Celts; . . . the third, due to Professor Rhys, is that the Picts were non-Aryans, whose language was overlaid by loans from Welsh and Irish; and the fourth, held by two of the most eminent Celtic scholars of the day, Professor Windisch and Dr. Whitley Stokes, is that they were Celts, but more nearly allied to the Cymry than to the Gael. . . . The conclusion to which we come is that the Picts, whatever traces they show of a non-Aryan racial element, . . . spoke a Celtic language belonging to a branch of Celtic allied to the Cymric, . . . and that this dialect of the Gallo-Cymric stock was a wave of Celtic speech from the continent previous to the Gaulish which held England when Cæsar entered Britain.”

readings.text:
Ðā ongunnon twā ðēoda, Pihtas norðan, and Scottas westan, hīe onwinnan, and hiera ǣhta niman and hęrgian; and hīe fela gēara iermdon and hīendon. Ðā, on ðǣre unstilnesse, onsęndon hīe ǣrendwrecan tō Rome mid gewritum and wēpendre bēne; him fultumes bǣdon, and him gehēton ēaðmōde hīernesse and singāle underðēodnesse, gif hīe him gefultumoden ðæt hīe meahten hiera fīend oferwinnan. Ðā onsęndon hīe him micelne hęre tō fultume, and, sōna ðæs-ðe hīe on ðis īgland cōmon, ðā campedon hīe wið hiera fēondum, and him micel wæl ongeslōgon, and of hiera gemǣrum ādrifon and āflīemdon; and lǣrdon ðæt hīe fæsten worhten him tō gebeorge wið hiera fēondum; and swā, mid micle sige, hām fōron.

Ðā ðæt ðā ongēaton ðā ǣrran gewinnan, ðæt se Rōmanisca hęre wæs onweg gewiten, ðā cōmon hīe sōna mid sciphęre on hiera landgemǣru, and slōgon ealle and cwealdon ðæt hīe gemētton, and swā-swā rīpe ierðe fortrǣdon and fornōmon, and hīe mid ealle foriermdon.

local_support.learner_help: Ongunnon, began, takes the three infinitives onwinnan, attack, niman, take, and hęrgian, plunder. Pihtas are the Picts, Scottas the Scots; norðan and westan mean from the north and from the west. Hīe refers to the Britons introduced in the separate context; ǣhta means possessions.

Pihtas are the Picts, Scottas the Scots; norðan and westan mean from the north and from the west. Hīe refers to the Britons introduced in the separate context; ǣhta means possessions.

local_support.anchor_text: and hīe fela gēara iermdon and hīendon
local_support.learner_help: Iermdon and hīendon mean afflicted and oppressed. Fela gēara means for many years, with genitive after fela. Hīe can be the Britons as object with the raiders continuing as subject, or the raiders as subject with a Briton object understood; the events do not change. Do not infer a unique case from the spelling.

local_support.learner_help: On ðǣre unstilnesse, amid that unrest. Onsęndon is the exact prefixed sent; the Britons are now the subject. Ǣrendwrecan, messengers; tō Rome, to Rome. Mid gewritum and wēpendre bēne means with letters and a tearful petition. Wēpendre is a present participle, strong dative feminine singular agreeing with bēne.

local_support.learner_help: In him fultumes bǣdon, him names the Romans asked and fultumes is the genitive thing requested: help. Hīernes is obedience; singāl is continual; underðēodnes is subjection. Ēaðmōde and singāle are accusative feminine singular. The promise is made by the Britons to the Romans.

local_support.learner_help: Gefultumoden is a preterite subjunctive: if they, the Romans, would help them, the Britons. The following ðæt clause gives the purpose, so that they might overcome their enemies. Meahten is the known preterite subjunctive plural of magan; oferwinnan means overcome. This whole reported condition/purpose sequence is supported locally.

local_support.learner_help: Here the subject of onsęndon is the Romans, while him refers to the Britons. Tō fultume means as help/to their aid. The Old English says they sent an army in the active voice; Cook compares a passive Latin expression. Preserve the actual Old English voice when analyzing it.

local_support.learner_help: Sōna ðæs-ðe means as soon as. On ðis īgland has the accusative goal, to/onto this island. Hīe refers to the Roman force. The following ðā resumes the narrative.

local_support.learner_help: Campedon, fought; wið hiera fēondum, against their enemies, with the source dative after wið. Him micel wæl ongeslōgon means inflicted great slaughter on them. Of hiera gemǣrum means out of their borders, with dative after of; the borders belong to the Britons, Rome’s allies. Āflīemdon means put to flight, reinforcing ādrifon. The enemy object carries on through the coordinated verbs.

local_support.learner_help: Lǣrdon means advised/instructed. Fæsten is a fortification; worhten is the known unprefixed wyrcean preterite subjunctive, here make/build in the advice clause. Him tō gebeorge means for their own protection. The Romans give the advice and the Britons are to build. The source’s wið + dative remains locally supplied.

local_support.anchor_text: and swā, mid micle sige, hām fōron
local_support.learner_help: Sige means victory. Mid micle sige is with great victory: the adjective has the instrumental micle beside the dative noun, as Cook’s note directs. Treat this as a supplied source construction. Hām is the directional home, without a preposition.

local_support.anchor_text: Ðā ðæt ðā ongēaton ðā ǣrran gewinnan, ðæt
local_support.learner_help: Read the three ðā forms in order as when, then, the. The first ðæt is an anticipatory object, this/that, expanded by the later that-clause. Ongēaton means realized; ǣrran gewinnan means former enemies. Gewinnan is a weak masculine plural noun, distinct from the previously supplied neuter gewinn, trouble.

local_support.anchor_text: se Rōmanisca hęre wæs onweg gewiten
local_support.learner_help: Rōmanisca is the weak masculine adjective Roman. Wæs onweg gewiten means had gone away: gewiten is the past participle of intransitive gewītan. This is an intransitive completed-state/perfect expression, not a passive. The source has plain-e onweg; retain it beside the earlier selected onwęg.

local_support.anchor_text: slōgon ealle and cwealdon ðæt hīe gemētton
local_support.learner_help: Cwealdon means killed. Slōgon and cwealdon reinforce the attack. Ealle is all, naturally people in context; the following neuter ðæt is a headless/collective all that they encountered. A translation all they encountered need not pretend that ðæt is an overt masculine personal relative. Cook’s Latin note reads cædunt.

local_support.anchor_text: swā-swā rīpe ierðe fortrǣdon and fornōmon

actual_prior_record.description: Produce the selected article forms agreeing with their own noun in gender, number and nominative/genitive/dative/accusative case.
Produce limiting relational genitives. Follow Cook's exercise target: dependent first, head noun without its own article; retain the dependent's required article.
Use taught locative on with dative ('in/on'); this is a selected construction, not a universal spatial rule.
Use the copula's appropriate number/person in the taught ordinary clauses.

Accusative object with audited senses of hīeran, cyssan, sęttan, sęndan, lǣdan, mētan, nęrian, lufian, habban, gefyllan, gewyrcean, gefręmman, geblētsian, gehālgian and the thing given with sęllan. Not every weak verb governs accusative.
Independently formed sęllan: dative recipient, accusative thing, noun/pronoun arguments. No sęndan recipient government inferred.
Use nominative subjects and governed object/recipient cases; grammatical gender/number tracks referents, including inanimate nouns. Syncretic spelling alone does not settle antecedence.
his/hiere/hiera are invariant possessors; possessor reference determines choice, while the head keeps its own case/number.
Selected adverbs qualify actions or whole statements without case/number/gender agreement; sōðlice truly is distinct from the supplied source connective sense.
Adjectives agree with their own noun/referent in case, number and gender; attributive and ordinary positive predicate uses are taught.
Cardinal one with singular nouns, 2–12 with plural count nouns; numeral gender/case agrees where the selected system inflects.
Checked cardinal 4–12 forms used invariantly before plural count nouns; no postposed/substantival inflection or higher-number partitive syntax.
Complete ān singular cardinal forms with singular count nouns; plural reference cells confer no productive plural-one sense.
Complete twēgen/ðrīe N/G/D/A plural across genders; no noun dual paradigm.
Bounded subject A + copula + comparative + ðonne + parallel subject B: B is nominative, with repeated copula understood. No generalized comparative-clause or genitive-standard syntax.

Ordinary attributive adjectives are weak after article/demonstrative; bare ordinary adjectives are strong. After possessives Cook permits strong and sometimes weak; no universal possessive→weak rule and no new rule for adjectives after limiting genitives.
The six agreeing possessives have complete strong morphology. Their endings agree with the possessed noun, not the possessor; personal-genitive citations retain separate records.
Ordinary positive predicative adjectives are strong and nominative, agreeing with the subject even when its noun phrase contains an article. Comparatives remain weak.
Complete selected strong N/G/D/A singular/plural in all genders; lexical alternations and distinct reference instrumentals are identified.
Complete selected weak N/G/D/A singular/plural; ordinary genitive plural -ra and explicitly audited comparative exceptions.
Selected ordinary transitive uses: drīfan drives cattle, bindan binds an animal, cēosan chooses a thing, findan finds a thing and drincan drinks water; the direct object is accusative.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Exact lexical government is independently evidenced. Cattle, an animal, ships and dwellings in these new compositions are declared ordinary lexical applications, not falsely attributed source quotations. No universal strong-verb accusative rule.

actual_prior_record.description: Helpan takes the dative being or recipient helped in the selected ordinary use. The attested person examples support the declared new application to birds.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Dative being/recipient is the selected target. Attested human examples support the explicitly declared ordinary lexical application to birds. The documented genitive alternative is valid but is not the construction requested here.

actual_prior_record.description: Use the assigned strong preterites for successive past events in independent coordinated clauses, retaining prior subject agreement and direct quotation.
Beran in carry and niman in take have an accusative person/thing as their selected ordinary object.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: The new food/fish examples are declared ordinary lexical applications, not falsely attributed source quotations; no goal or source preposition is introduced.

actual_prior_record.description: Geswīcan governs the genitive of the work/action from which the subject ceases.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: English from is represented by the checked governed genitive here; no unassigned fram-phrase is substituted.

actual_prior_record.description: Cweðan introduces direct quoted speech with an independent finite clause; quoted first-person reference belongs to the quoted speaker.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Explicit extension of the earlier sęcgan quotation frame; content clauses, reported speech and requests remain outside production.

actual_prior_record.description: Sittan, licgan and standan describe ordinary intransitive posture; a previously taught locative on+dative phrase may locate the subject.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: No causal placement, directional complement or stand-against construction is inferred.

actual_prior_record.description: Sēon and gesēon take an accusative person/thing in the selected ordinary see use.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Their source content clauses remain supplied; no infinitive-of-perception or general complement rule.

actual_prior_record.description: Cuman means come in an ordinary intransitive clause and supplies the movement verb before the selected same-subject purpose infinitive.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: No unassigned destination phrase or sense of becuman follows.

actual_prior_record.description: The prior cweðan direct-quotation frame now also introduces the independently taught second-person commands. Quoted reference belongs to the speaker/addressee context.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Only the expressly selected forms, senses and constructions are assigned.

actual_prior_record.description: Faran means go/travel in an ordinary intransitive clause and as the action in the newly taught volitional complement.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: No destination, vehicle, motion-preposition or sailing sense is implied.

actual_prior_record.description: Second-singular commands address one person; plural commands address two or more, without a separate dual ending. The subject can remain unexpressed in the selected direct instructions.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: These are second-person commands, not third-person optative wishes or a new general politeness system.

actual_prior_record.description: The finite modal/volitional verb carries subject agreement; its selected plain infinitive does not acquire person/number endings or tō in the taught construction.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Only the expressly selected forms, senses and constructions are assigned.

actual_prior_record.description: Willan plus a plain infinitive expresses desire or willingness; wolde can state past desire without asserting that the desired act occurred.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Only the expressly selected forms, senses and constructions are assigned.

actual_prior_record.description: Open gif clauses can use indicative. A contextually tentative/hypothetical request can use present subjunctive, followed by an imperative or ordinary indicative main clause. Gif itself never licenses an automatic conversion rule.

Keep learned mæg capability, mōt permission, wille/wolde volition distinct from inflectional subjunctive wishes. A past spelling does not mechanically mean English would/might; willan is not automatically future. Preserve bounded earlier cunnan/ðurfan/durran/sculan senses.

For assigned accusative-object verbs, present or preterite wesan/bēon or weorðan + past participle expresses passive. Finite auxiliary agrees with the nominative subject. Agent omitted in productive tasks; no new fram-agent rule needed. Wesan often presents state/result and weorðan event, but not an absolute contrast or one-to-one English tense mapping.
In verbal predicates a past participle may be uninflected or take strong-masculine-like endings: neuter plural dēor bunden/bundene are both licensed. Attributive agreement remains a different target.

Independent present subjunctive expresses wishes/exhortations, including thirdperson Let... and firstplural Letus.... Secondperson imperative and subjunctive are formally/syntactically distinct even where spellings coincide. English let here is not a new lǣtan causative construction.

Direct yes/no questions commonly begin with the finite verb; wh-words or phrases commonly precede the finite verb, and a wh-subject is itself the subject. No English dummy do is added. These are tendencies, not an exceptionless V2 transformation.
The inflected se/sēo/ðæt series can introduce relative clauses alone or followed by ðe; reuse its full NGDA morphology with newly taught relative function.

In selected productive relative clauses, gender and number track the antecedent while relative case is governed by its function within its own clause. An antecedent in dative can have a nominative relative, and vice versa; this is the selected ordinary construction, not a universal ban on attraction.
Invariant ðe introduces an ordinary relative clause and can represent different internal case functions; it is not an English personal interrogative pronoun.
A finite content clause introduced by invariant ðæt fills the content complement of the selected knowing/saying verb.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Keep distinct from determiner/relative ðæt; clause has its own subject and finite verb.

actual_prior_record.description: Mid + dative names an accompanying person or cargo.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Means/manner/abstract circumstance require their own prior or supplied records.

actual_prior_record.description: Reported content commonly uses subjunctive; a proposition asserted as fact may use indicative.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Exercises must name the communicative stance when a specific mood is required; subjunctive does not mean the report is false.

actual_prior_record.description: Use the nominative-shaped noun in direct address; an accompanying adjective is weak. Thus the morphology of the noun follows number and its own class, while good in O good fellows/workmen uses weak plural. Ēalā is an optional interjection where the original English says O.

actual_prior_record.scope_note: Do not infer micel +mass or general noun-of-measure syntax.

actual_prior_record.description: Gewītan means depart/go away and may take fram+dative source.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Not the distinct short-vowel preterite-present know.

actual_prior_record.description: Hwonne introduces a direct when-question using ordinary finite interrogative syntax.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: No temporal subordinate when-clause system is introduced.

actual_prior_record.description: Present indicative can refer to future events where context supplies futurity; English will/shall need not produce willan.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Willan remains volitional where intention is meant; no new periphrastic future tense.

actual_prior_record.description: The selected weak adjectives with the article can name people: the hungry, naked, sick, unrighteous; case and number follow their clause role.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Plural people and an adjective modifying an expressed singular person must be distinguished. Do not imply every abstract substantive use is covered.

actual_prior_record.description: Tō+dative gives a destination with come/go/fly.
actual_prior_record.scope_note: Separate from tō purpose/function and tō+inflected infinitive.

audited_inflection_rules.description: Full NGDA noun systems apply the image-checked stem and declared class. Gehīersumnes and ręst have singular abstract production; plural morphology is recognition reference without a new count sense.

Fōt has fēt in selected dative singular and nominative/accusative plural; fōt- in other ending-bearing cells. Fōte is an accepted dative alternative and fōtas an occasional plural, not the selected recall form.

Fēond has selected fēonde dative singular, fīend nominative/accusative plural and fēonda genitive plural. Cook and Wright document other dative/plural realizations; do not substitute the genitive -endra of a different -end family.

Hęre and sciphęre have the complete selected ordinary -e masculine pattern. Cook44.2 explicitly permits expanded hęrg-/hęrig- before singular endings and hęrg-/hęrig-/hęrige- before plural endings; apply the same rule within sciphęre. Variants are accepted without testing independent recall.

Ēðel, sāwol and wǣpen have ending-bearing ēðl-, sāwl- and wǣpn-. Hærfest and pęning retain the medial vowel; the short second syllable is required for the ordinary syncope rule. Wǣpnu is the selected plural beside explicit wǣp(e)n alternatives.
Andwlita and sǣdtīma use the weak masculine pattern. Fǣmne and heorte use the weak feminine pattern, with fǣmn- and heort- before endings. Gehīersumnes doubles final s before endings.

Brād, beald, earg, ēaðmōd and mildheort use the complete long strong model and the weak model. Īsern and ēadig use the selected disyllabic short-model endings, retaining their medial vowel; ēadig has expressly documented optional syncope. Strong/weak choice and ordinary agreement remain prior rules.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Strong indicative systems
audited_inflection_rules.rule: The present singular uses -e, -st, -ð and plural -að, subject to stated stem/dental changes. Preterite first/third singular share the selected singular stem; second singular uses the plural stem with -e; all plural persons use -on. Ādrīfan has ī/ā/i; gehātan retains ge- and selects hā-/hēt-, with hǣt- in second/third present singular. Flēon is contracted: flēo-, flīeh-, flēah-, flug- are explicitly distributed, not mechanically generated from the citation.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Weak I selected systems
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Gemētan and grētan retain ē; t before the third-singular dental yields selected -tt, and the preterite is -tte/-ttest/-tton. Ēhtan has ēht in third present singular and ēhte/-est/-on in the preterite, not an invented doubled dental. Cȳðan selects cȳst and cȳð after regular dental interaction; cȳðde/-dest/-don is selected, with attested cȳdde variants recognized. These are complete present/preterite indicative systems only.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Weak II selected systems
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Geopenian and leornian have -ie, -ast, -að, -iað in the present, and -ode, -odest, -ode, -odon in the preterite. The plural form serves all persons; each person/number coordinate is still displayed.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Āgan positive indicative
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Āh/āhst/āh and plural āgon form the present; āhte/āhtest/āhte and plural āhton form the preterite. These cells are the full defined positive indicative. Supplied nāh does not establish a negative paradigm.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Nine complete direct-command pairs
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Both singular and plural are provided for sęndan, bringan, ādrīfan, flēon, gemētan, geopenian, weorpan, leornian and rīsan. Strong long stems and long weak I stems use the selected bare singular; contracted flēon has flēoh; weak II uses -a singular and -iað plural. The commands do not imply newly productive subjunctives.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Five complete base pairs with unequal learning scope
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Gewyrcean/gewyrcende/geworht, gierwan/gierwende/gierwed and sęttan/sęttende/sętt have productive present and past bases; their larger syntactic uses remain separately bounded. Gewītan/gewītende/gewiten and sittan/sittende/seten are recognition/reference pairs. A displayed participle base is not a complete adjectival declension or an unrestricted perfect/progressive system.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Two complete plain/inflected shape pairs
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Ādrīfan/ādrīfanne and genēosian/genēosianne show both shapes. Plain infinitives are productive only with the already taught specified modals; inflected shapes are recognition/reference.

audited_inflection_rules.title: Twelve construction positions, not twelve inflectional cells
audited_inflection_rules.rule: The complete present and preterite habban construction display has six person/number positions for each tense and binds prior finite auxiliary forms, prior accusative ðæt hūs and new productive geworht. Count these as construction examples separately; do not fabricate multiword lexical forms. The finite auxiliary agrees with the subject; the object is the participle patient.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Finite habban with a selected transitive past participle expresses a completed action or present/past result.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: The auxiliary agrees with the subject, while the accusative object is the patient of the participle. Selected bare participles are productive. Object-agreeing alternatives are recognized/accepted only within independently supported inflection; no arbitrary causative or intransitive have-perfect is introduced.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Recognize wesan with an intransitive past participle, specifically gewiten.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: The subject is the departing participant; the phrase is not passive merely because it contains be. Recognize the contextual completed-departure meaning; no unrestricted productive system.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Recognize wesan with a present participle, specifically sittende.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Context may motivate simple, progressive or durative English. A simple finite Old English verb may also receive progressive English. No obligatory modern progressive category is inferred.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Compare an active transitive clause with a supported agentless passive and distinguish event from resulting state.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Retains prior u07-passive: a passive subject is the affected entity; converting to agentless passive omits any named active agent. Wearð may focus on coming into the condition, wæs on a state or contextually an event. No mechanical became/was rule or fram-agent production.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Express simultaneous, anterior and intended-later time relative to a reporting viewpoint.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Prior report subjunctives provide simultaneous sīe/wǣre; anterior hæfde plus selected participle is new. Hæfde is syncretic and context identifies the report function. Wolde plus infinitive retains volition/intention and does not guarantee later realization. Indicative reports may be defensible; no automatic backshift or subjunctive=false.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Intransitive cease/fail without an expressed genitive object, including seedtime and harvest ceasing or failing in Cook19.16. Earlier genitive cessation remains available for ceasing from rule.
Accusative person killed; distinguishes this lethal sense from previously taught strike/smite.
Seeing is asserted absolutely in the bounded temporal clauses of Cook20.2; no accusative object must be invented.
On+dative with rich/lowly predicates; not physical motion into the noun.
Beforan+dative marks the person before whom someone is sent; extends earlier static location explicitly.
Accusative thing prepared; with the selected past participle, habban retains that accusative patient.
Accusative text or letter written; prior morphology does not itself establish this lexical frame.
Accusative person/thing sent and dative recipient; beforan+dative is a separate ahead-of frame.
Accusative thing thrown, including the assigned hook.
Welig on+dative identifies the thing or resource in which a person, place or productive event is rich; includes harvest rich in fruit.
Ābūtan+accusative, surrounding a person/thing or building around it.
Selected accusative after sending among a group; the directly attested sheep/wolves passage supports this precise use. Dative location is also attested but is not the selected productive frame.
Æt+dative marks the person from whom one learns, as in leornian æt a person.
For+dative identifies the beneficiary in the assigned payment/giving expression; not every for-case or causal use.
Accusative quantity of time expresses duration.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: The supplied forty-years phrase is explicitly local support; this does not establish all numeral systems.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: A numeral plus genitive measure noun can state breadth or height.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: The measure noun fōt is separately taught in full; the twenty-feet quantity remains supplied local support.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Nǣfre and preverbal ne reinforce one negative meaning.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Bounded never/never again constructions only; nǣfre mā means never more/again. Do not teach a general negative-pronoun family by implication.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Predicative genitive identifies a possessor; predicative possessive adjectives agree with what is possessed.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Distinguish an owner in genitive from ðīn in the gender/number of dæg or niht. Earlier attributive forms are reused with an explicit new syntax milestone.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Quantitative predicative mā means more in number with a plural subject.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Selected indeclinable mā plus prior ðonne comparison standard; distinct from earlier adverbial amount of doing. No new māran comparative-adjective system is required.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: On+accusative with adjectival ōðer may have an understood city noun.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Supplied local on ōðre [ceastre] analysis, using the actual prior ceaster system; no unrestricted nominal ellipsis production is inferred.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Two separated swā tokens express equality of degree.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: First swā is degree; second swā introduces the standard. Bind each to the actual prior swa-invariant form and its new sense; do not invent a compound form spanning the intervening adjective.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Swā plus a nominal compares the persons sent to sheep.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Explicit bounded extension beyond the prior finite comparative clause.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Recognize the selected past reported condition and possibility in the Picts and Scots passage.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Source-specific gif ... gefultumoden and ðæt ... meahten are supplied/analyzed in context. This does not promote a complete new conditional or modal subjunctive system.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Finding accusative rest may include the dative beneficiaries.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Declared application of Cook160–161 general dative-of-benefit syntax to the bounded Cook21.9 requirement; not a separately quoted dictionary valency witness. It does not require a preposition translating English unto.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Supplied nāh for the negative possession clause in Cook20.4.
audited_inflection_rules.scope_and_limits: Reuse already supplied nis for the other local negative clause; full negative systems are not production.

Accusative thing learned when expressed; æt+dative identifies the person from whom one learns. Objectless learn from me is independently evidenced.

limits: The actual eleven-unit baseline alone establishes prior teaching.
Present and preterite are morphological categories; context supplies temporal relations and English translation.
Productive habban compounds use an accusative object and selected uninflected participle bases; the indicative construction display does not invent new inflected words or exhaust all moods.
Reported anterior compounds reuse prior subjunctive morphology; reported simultaneous, anterior and intended later events are distinguished without mechanical backshift.
Wesan with intransitive past participles and present participles is newly assigned for recognition, with contextual interpretation.
Complete participle bases do not assign unlisted adjective declensions or unrestricted auxiliary selection.
Recognition number counterparts, adjective instrumental reference cells and exact supplied source spellings retain their separate scope.
The exact connected source span preserves both paragraphs, all21 attached original notes and source spelling.
Source aids remain visible during supported tasks and never become unaided-recall targets.

The selected gemētt cell is present indicative third singular. Explain preterite gemētte without copying the lexical-audit contrast note about an unassigned gemētan past participle into learner prose. No gemētan participle system or extra supplied citation is assigned.
review_independence: The reserved reviewer receives public tasks and unordered dependency sets. A disclosed answer-bearing message exposed EX-VI-21-04 only; no private files were opened. Their independent solve therefore covers75 unexposed tasks. A fresh unexposed reviewer must solve EX-VI-21-04 and freeze that solution before key access. All private files remain excluded until the corresponding independent solutions are frozen.

reviewer_exposure.cause: A source-editor coordination message included the proposed answer clause; the recipient promptly disclosed it.
